analysis.one_liner: Creates universal government-guaranteed health coverage for every U.S. resident, funded by new payroll and income taxes, replacing Medicare, Medicaid, and employer insurance.
analysis.headline: The bill won a committee report in the House in July 1994 but never received a vote in the full House or the Senate, and the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995 with the bill dead.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have guaranteed comprehensive health coverage — hospital care, doctors, prescription drugs, mental health, dental care for children, long-term care — to every U.S. resident, with no deductibles or copayments for acute and preventive care. States would run the program under a national board's standards, paid for by an 8.4% tax on employers' payrolls (4% for small employers), a 2.1% tax on individuals' income, and higher taxes on tobacco and firearms. Medicare, Medicaid, federal employee coverage, and private insurance that duplicates the program would all be phased out. The bill was sent to six House committees; only one, Education and Labor, ever reported it back, and the full House never voted.
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. resident would gain guaranteed comprehensive coverage with free choice of provider and no out-of-pocket charges for acute or preventive care [S2]. People currently uninsured or underinsured, families facing medical bills, and patients paying for prescriptions would all be covered automatically at birth or upon becoming a lawful resident [S2]. Rural and underserved communities would see targeted grants and payment incentives to attract providers [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Entitles every citizen, national, and lawful resident alien to comprehensive health services — hospital care, practitioner services, preventive care, long-term care, prescription drugs, dental, mental health, and substance abuse treatment — starting January 1, 1996 [S2].
Prohibits all deductibles, coinsurance, and copayments for acute and preventive benefits, and bars providers from charging patients anything for covered services [S2].
Automatically enrolls people at birth or upon gaining lawful resident status, makes benefits portable across states, and caps any waiting period at three months [S2].
Replaces Medicare, Medicaid, the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program, and CHAMPUS with a single program, while leaving veterans' VA and Indian Health Service benefits untouched [S2].
Directs new grants and payment incentives toward community health centers, school-based health sites, and care in medically underserved urban and rural areas [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers would pay a payroll excise tax of 8.4% of wages (4% for small employers under 75 employees averaging under $24,000 in wages), individuals would pay a 2.1% income tax with no credits, and tobacco and firearms would face higher excise taxes — including a 50% tax on firearms sales [S2]. Private insurers would lose the market for coverage that duplicates program benefits [S2]. Hospitals and other facilities would shift from billing insurers to operating under state-approved annual global budgets, capping their revenue [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers, earners, tobacco and gun sellers

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes substantial new taxes: an 8.4% employer payroll tax, a 2.1% tax on individual income with no credits allowed, higher tobacco taxes, and a 50% manufacturer tax on firearms and ammunition [S2].
It bans the sale of private health insurance that duplicates program benefits, ending coverage arrangements many people have through employers or unions [S2].

A national board would set practice guidelines, an approved-drug list with negotiated maximum prices, and coverage limits — including utilization-review thresholds for mental health care and quantity limits on eyeglasses, hearing aids, and durable equipment — concentrating major coverage decisions in a federal body [S2].

Dental coverage would exclude orthodontia and, in the introduced version, cover treatment for dental disease only for children under 18; home and community-based long-term care payments would be capped at 65% of the cost of nursing home care [S2].

Hospitals and facilities would operate under annual prospective global budgets, a payment system that guarantees funding but caps what facilities can spend and earn, with capital spending subject to regional planning approval [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a sweeping benefit — universal, no-cost-sharing coverage of nearly all medical needs — at the cost of a large new tax burden on employers and wage earners and the elimination of private duplicate coverage. Its centralized design (a national board setting budgets, payment rates, practice guidelines, and a drug formulary) was its biggest design risk: it aimed to control costs by capping what hospitals and providers could be paid, which supporters saw as the only real way to finance universal coverage and critics saw as rationing by bureaucracy. Whether the global-budget and global-budget-plus-fee-schedule payment systems would have preserved access without long waits was the central untested question; the bill never got far enough to be judged in practice.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to six House committees when introduced; only the Education and Labor Committee ever reported it back, on July 22, 1994, and the full House and the Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Rep. George Miller introduced the American Health Security Act of 1994 in the House on March 3, 1994, joined by 13 Democratic cosponsors [S1][S5].
On introduction day it was referred to six committees: Armed Services, Education and Labor, Energy and Commerce, Natural Resources, Post Office and Civil Service, and Ways and Means [S6].

The bill was then split among nine subcommittees across those committees; three Education and Labor subcommittees held mark-up sessions and forwarded an amended bill to the full committee in June 1994 [S6].
The full Education and Labor Committee marked it up, ordered it reported, and reported it amended (H. Rept. 103-618, Part I) on July 22, 1994 — the only committee action completing [S3][S6].
No other committee reported the bill, the House never took it up, and no further action occurred before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S1][S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers, employers who would have owed the new payroll tax, and providers opposed to global budgets and price controls were better off because the bill died — the existing insurance-based system continued. The roughly 15% of Americans then uninsured gained nothing from the outcome.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers, employers, and the status quo

for.name: Rep. George Miller
for.what_they_did: Introduced the American Health Security Act of 1994 in the House and led it through the Education and Labor Committee, which he sat on.

for.name: 13 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Jim McDermott, Xavier Becerra, and others listed on the introduction [S4][S5].

for.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
for.what_they_did: Held subcommittee and full-committee mark-ups, amended the bill, and reported it to the House on July 22, 1994.

against.name: House Committees on Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce
against.role: Committees with jurisdiction over Medicare, Medicaid, and employer health benefits
against.what_they_did: Received referrals of the bill on March 3, 1994, sent it to subcommittees, and never reported it, keeping the financing-heavy titles from advancing [S6].

against.name: House Committee on Armed Services, Post Office and Civil Service, and Natural Resources
against.what_they_did: Received referrals and took subcommittee-level action or none, but never reported the bill back to the House [S6].

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.role: Speaker and majority leadership of the 103rd Congress
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a House floor vote in 1994, as the chamber's attention stayed on the Clinton administration's competing health plan; no floor action of any kind appears in the record [S6].

against.name: Health insurance industry
against.what_they_did: Funded a large public advertising campaign against government-run universal coverage during the 1994 health care debate, which targeted the entire single-payer approach this bill embodied.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat — 14 House Democrats in all, no Republicans — and the bill died in a Democratic-controlled Congress without ever reaching a floor vote.

industries.note: The bill bans the sale of private insurance that duplicates program benefits and supersedes the employer-coverage system insurers administer, effectively ending their core market [S2]. Insurers' business of covering ordinary Americans is replaced by a public program [S2].

Facilities would be locked in as the program's delivery channel, paid through state-approved annual global budgets with guaranteed public funding — but their revenue would be capped by those budgets and their capital spending would go through regional planning approval [S2].

Practitioners would get guaranteed fee-for-service payment directly from state programs and could never bill patients for covered services — no more uninsured patients or bad debt, but no balance billing either, and payment rates set by negotiated fee schedules under a national budget cap [S2].
A national board would publish an approved-drug list and negotiate maximum prices with manufacturers, replacing today's largely unregulated pricing [S2].

Excise taxes on tobacco products would rise, and manufacturers or importers would pay a 50% tax on the sale of pistols, revolvers, firearms, shells, and cartridges, with the revenue funding the program [S2].
Employers would pay an 8.4% payroll tax (4% for small ones), but would be freed from administering health benefits, and employer plans could no longer duplicate the program [S2].
